fonte: SLEEP
titulo: Beyond automation: what’s next for artificial intelligence in sleep?
resumo: Sleep is a foundational pillar of health [1], deeply linked to cognitive function [2], metabolism [3], and mental health [4]. Yet, sleep disorders remain a pervasive global health issue [5], often underdiagnosed and inadequately managed [6]. Polysomnography (PSG), the gold standard for sleep assessment, requires specialized facilities and personnel, making it costly, inconvenient, and inaccessible for many. Addressing these limitations, artificial intelligence (AI) is being increasingly applied to challenges in sleep medicine. While often associated colloquially with large language models (LLMs), its broader definition encompasses computational systems designed to learn from data to perform tasks that typically require human intelligence. For sleep analysis, one of the earliest and most impactful applications of AI has been to automate the scoring of sleep stages from PSG data. Indeed, studies utilizing deep neural networks [7, 8] demonstrated that AI models can match human expert accuracy [9]. However, the contribution of AI extends beyond simply automating the task of manual sleep scoring. For example, AI models can provide probabilistic outputs for each sleep stage per epoch, rather than a single deterministic label. This has given rise to novel representations like the hypnodensity graph [10], which offers richer information than the traditional hypnogram. This allows clinicians and researchers to quantify stage uncertainty and derive novel features for diagnosing sleep disorders. Furthermore, AI models can enable analysis at temporal resolutions finer than the conventional 30-s epoch. For instance, Perslev et al. [11] introduced a model capable of high-frequency sleep staging (up to 1280 stages/minute) and found that these granular sleep stages allowed for better separation of healthy controls versus apnea patients. Another avenue involves probing the internal representations, or “embeddings,” learned by these AI models. Studies analyzing these embeddings suggest that sleep physiology may exist on a continuum rather than five discrete categories. For example, work on wearable electroencephalography (EEG) data revealed potential sub-clusters within N2 sleep and a continuous mapping between sleep states [12], findings echoed in earlier studies using clinical electroencephalography (EEG) [13]. These initial successes primarily relied on supervised learning, in which the AI model was trained on input examples paired with their correct output labels. Unfortunately, the reliance on data labeled by human experts restricts the scale of data available for training sophisticated models. Meanwhile, vast unlabeled physiological data exist—an underutilized resource. More recently, self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a promising approach specifically designed to make use of these data. SSL leverages the inherent structure of the signals, training models on specific “pre-text” tasks—for instance, predicting a masked portion of an EEG signal based on its surrounding context. The resulting “foundation models” learn effective and general-purpose representations of the underlying physiological data which can then be adapted for specific “downstream” tasks, such as sleep staging, or apnea detection, either by using their learned embeddings (“feature extraction”) or by further training the model on a smaller labeled dataset (“fine-tuning”). This approach shares similarities with the major advancements seen with LLMs, which are pre-trained on large volumes of internet text to learn the underlying structure of language before being fine-tuned for specific applications. In the EEG domain, Banville et al. [14] were some of the first to demonstrate that fine-tuned pre-trained models significantly outperform models trained from scratch on downstream tasks, especially when labeled data are scarce. This result was also seen in another study [15] with an AI model based on the transformer architecture [16], the backbone of modern language and vision models. The potential of foundation models grows further when incorporating multi-modal data. Thapa et al. developed SleepFM [17], a foundation model trained on EEG, electrocardiography (ECG), and respiratory signals. They showed that a simple Logistic Regression classifier trained on representations learned by SleepFM outperformed supervised neural networks for tasks like sleep staging and sleep-disordered breathing detection. A recent study by Fox et al. [18] represents a notable contribution to this rapidly evolving field. They introduce PFTSleep, a model based on the PatchTST design [19] originally used for time-series forecasting. For developing PFTSleep, the authors utilized data from 13 888 recordings gathered from the Sleep Heart Health Study, the Osteoporotic Fractures in Men Study visit 1 (MrOS-1), and Wisconsin Sleep Cohort. The model processed seven input channels (EEG, electrooculography (EOG), electromyography (EMG), ECG, SpO2, along with thorax and abdomen respiration signals), and its embeddings fed a separate recurrent network trained for stage classification. On held-out test data, the reported performance matched or exceeded human inter-rater reliability benchmarks for sleep staging. PFTSleep was then evaluated on three external datasets: MrOS-2 (a longitudinal follow-up of MrOS-1), the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA), and the Apnea Positive Pressure Long-term Efficacy Study (APPLES). On the MrOS-2 data, the model exceeded expert-level performance with a Cohen’s Kappa of 0.82, suggesting applicability for monitoring sleep changes over time. Performance on the MESA and APPLES datasets was lower, yielding Cohen’s Kappa values of 0.60 and 0.59, respectively. However, re-training the classifier using MESA data improved the Kappa score on that dataset to 0.76. Interestingly, re-training the core PFTSleep model did not result in a similar improvement, suggesting that the cross-dataset performance differences relate more to labeling patterns than to PFTSleep feature generalizability. Similar analysis for the APPLES dataset was not reported. The authors also experimented with a 3-channel version of PFTSleep (EEG, EOG, and EMG) and found minimal but dataset-specific changes in sleep staging performance. For example, the 7-channel model performed better on MESA, but slightly worse on APPLES. This result is not surprising, since state-of-the-art results had been previously achieved with even a single channel of EEG [20]. However, the 7-channel representations, while not necessarily improving staging accuracy, might offer benefits for other downstream tasks. In fact, while achieving robust, generalizable automated scoring remains a key objective, the true promise of SSL and foundation models lies in the power of the representations they learn. Refining the SleepFM model [21], the authors utilize over 585 000 hours of PSG data across approximately 65 000 participants and predict the future onset of approximately 130 diseases with high accuracy (C-Index and Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUROC) ≥ 0.75), including neurological disorders, circulatory conditions, several cancers, and death. Such findings underscore the immense potential of leveraging foundation models for uncovering novel biomarkers predictive of future health risks. Furthermore, these advancements coincide with the proliferation of wearable biosensors, which are starting to offer promising alternatives for at-home sleep monitoring. Indeed, AI already demonstrates notable capabilities with wearables, enabling high-accuracy sleep staging via wearable EEG [22] and detecting sleep apnea [23]. The real inflection point, however, lies in the unprecedented scale of data acquisition possible with these wearables. This large volume of longitudinal data, considerably exceeding the reach of PSG studies, unlocks the ability to train next-generation AI foundation models and discover novel digital biomarkers beyond current capabilities. Looking ahead, what’s next for AI in sleep truly lies beyond mere automation. Crucially, the synergy between sophisticated AI and the growing availability of wearable technology paves the way for bringing personalized sleep assessment and monitoring into at-home settings, significantly enhancing both individual wellness and sleep research. While challenges in validation, accessibility, and ethical implementation remain, the current trajectory suggests that AI is set to reshape our understanding and management of sleep health in the coming years. Financial disclosure: Maurice Abou Jaoude is an employee at InteraXon Inc., a company involved in wearable EEG technology with applications in sleep, at the time of writing. Non-financial disclosure: none.

fonte: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
titulo: Securing Agentic AI Enterprise Workflows Against Prompt Injection Tool Poisoning Memory Manipulation and Excessive Agency Threats
resumo: Agentic artificial intelligence systems extend language models with planning, memory, tool invocation, data access, and autonomous action, creating enterprise capabilities that also expand the security boundary beyond prompt-response applications. This review examines how prompt injection, tool poisoning, memory manipulation, and excessive agency threaten agentic workflows across finance, healthcare, software development, customer operations, and critical business services. It analyzes direct and indirect prompt injection through user inputs, retrieved documents, webpages, emails, databases, and multimodal content, emphasizing how untrusted instructions can override policy or redirect plans. Tool poisoning is examined through malicious descriptions, compromised connectors, deceptive outputs, dependency tampering, and excessive permissions that enable unauthorized data access or transactions. The review further evaluates memory attacks through false fact insertion, persistence abuse, cross-session contamination, sensitive-data retention, and retrieval manipulation. Excessive agency is framed as a control failure arising when agents possess broad objectives, inadequate constraints, irreversible tools, or weak human oversight. Defensive approaches include instruction-data separation, contextual trust labeling, least-privilege authorization, capability-based tool access, schema validation, content sanitization, provenance tracking, memory partitioning, transactional safeguards, runtime policy enforcement, and human approval for consequential actions. Detection methods combining behavioral telemetry, execution graphs, anomaly scoring, canary resources, and policy-violation monitoring are compared using attack success rate, false alarms, intervention latency, task utility, and operational cost. The paper proposes a defense-in-depth framework spanning design-time threat modeling, pre-execution validation, constrained planning, monitored tool use, post-action verification, and recoverable state management. Key challenges include adaptive adversaries, ambiguous instruction hierarchies, third-party integrations, long-horizon attacks, evaluation realism, and the trade-off between autonomy and control. The review argues that secure enterprise deployment requires treating agentic artificial intelligence as a privileged software actor whose intentions, capabilities, memory, actions, and consequences must remain authenticated, bounded,

fonte: Clinical Chemistry
titulo: Generative Artificial Intelligence: More of the Same or Off the Control Chart?
resumo: Artificial intelligence (AI) involves a machine or computer performing tasks that typically require a human. Generative AI is a subtype of AI that outputs novel content, like text, speech, or pictures. Recent advances include the development of generative pre-trained transformers (GPTs), which are powerful large language models that have billions of parameters, trained on massive amounts of existing text. ChatGPT is a service OpenAI provider that allows users to dialog with its GPT model. It has gained much attention due to its remarkable ability to engage in human-like conversation and to produce sophisticated responses to prompts across wide-ranging content domains. In this article, our panel of experts delve into the various ways ChatGPT can be applied in clinical chemistry and medicine. They discuss the benefits and challenges of incorporating such technology into the medical field, including ethical concerns around privacy and data security. Overall, the panel discussion provides perspective on the future of medicine with ChatGPT and what this could mean for patients and healthcare providers. What is a generative AI model (as in ChatGPT), and what does it do? Jonathan H. Chen: A reductive description would be that these foundation models and large language models are “autocomplete on steroids,” similar to how your internet search bar guesses the next word based on statistical parameters, encoding probabilities of how often those sequences appeared in the past. Through sheer brute scale, the basic concept of these systems has been pushed to learning not millions of statistical parameters but to hundreds of billions of parameters about word relationships from billions of sources all over the internet (e.g., every published book, every Wikipedia and newspaper article, every PubMed abstract, every Twitter, and Reddit conversation, and much more). Many (including myself) have been surprised with the emergent properties these systems are developing with just sheer scale. The basic concept of autocomplete (guess the next word) ends up manifesting state-of-the-art capabilities in many higher-level tasks like summarization, translation, and question-answering. Applied to masses of available image data, generative systems are increasingly able to generate realistic and surprisingly adept images. Jason Baron: While the detailed technical underpinnings of ChatGPT itself have not been released, in general, large language models are at their core generative AI models that function as “fancy autocomplete.” That is, they sequentially “predict” the next word or token in a text response, using probabilistic sampling to make responses varied and nondeterministic. One way to think about generative AI is by comparing it to more traditional “discriminative” machine learning. A trained discriminative model takes a set of inputs (“X”) to “predict” an output (“Y”). For example, the inputs might be a set of laboratory test results or the pixel values for an image, and the model might predict whether the patient has sepsis. At a functional level, generative AI in some ways works in reverse, inputting a label or classification (Y) and then finding a set of data (X) that corresponds to this. Is this a transformative technology or a parlor trick? Jonathan H. Chen: This is a trick in that the underlying systems arguably do not actually think, understand, or know anything. However, the emergent properties at scale are becoming increasingly adept at higher level tasks to the point that it is becoming hard to distinguish human- from computer-generated content. I don’t believe AI robots are going to be taking over the planet anytime soon, but these do reflect an actively disruptive technology likely to permanently change the way we live and work. I would liken it to the advent of internet search, which completely changed the value of memorizing knowledge and instead shifted toward skills around rapidly searching through and appraising masses of information. Any task that revolves around producing, reading, editing, or otherwise manipulating language and images is likely to be approached very differently in the coming years. Brian Jackson: It has some elements of both transformative technology and parlor trick. Large language models might turn out to be transformative for some applications, such as language translation. It’s far from certain that large language models will be more generally transformative, even if other forms of AI are transformative. In particular, I’m skeptical that we’ll see wholesale replacement of human experts in the near future. As to the parlor trick question, the essence of parlor tricks is entertainment through deception. Chatbots likewise have a large element of deception, regardless of whether that’s the intent of their designers. Because building relationships through dialog is so deeply hardwired into the human brain and chatbots do a credible job of participating in dialog (even if it’s at a surface level), they trigger an unconscious sense of trust in the reader which is both unwarranted and dangerous. Essentially the human feels a human-like connection with the bot, and the emotions in turn subconsciously affect their logical thoughts. In some ways it’s a bit like the way people anthropomorphize their pets due to the ways in which the pets’ faces and actions connect with the emotional center of the brain. Assuming there is no further improvement in the technology beyond its capabilities today, how could we use these models in laboratory practice? Brian Jackson: Chatbots can be useful writing partners as long as a human takes ownership over the final edits. They could also be useful for low-stakes information retrieval tasks where you don’t need high levels of accuracy, particularly if the answers can be easily fact-checked. Jason Baron: We have to think about the question from the standpoint of not only what these models can theoretically do but what they can be trusted to do. Current models “hallucinate,” sometimes providing information that is fictitious yet plausible and convincing. Any hallucination rate significantly greater than zero would be too high for most clinical models where model outputs are going directly to end users without human review. However, hallucination may not be terrible, if the AI only drafts initial reports, notes, or other text and “in the loop” qualified healthcare professionals carefully check and edit the AI's initial draft. Thus, we could imagine, for example, an AI application that auto-generates a first draft of the pathologist interpretations that get appended to certain complex laboratory tests. Hallucination in this case might not cause clinical harm, if a pathologist were to carefully check and edit the model's initial draft as needed. However, whether the model is useful in practice for the application would then become an empiric question requiring the evaluation of factors including (a) whether the model still saves time after factoring in the time the pathologist takes to check the results and (b) how the accuracy of a pathologist working with a model check compares to that of a pathologist working alone. Current AI models might also find viable applications in tasks like workflow support if the clinical consequences of an error would be low. Jonathan H. Chen: Caveats abound, but many tasks based on manipulating the language of existing documents are now feasible in a way that was out of reach just a few years ago: produce a summary description for a laboratory specimen; translate that description into other languages for different patients to understand; adapt a log of laboratory processes into a draft of a standard operating manual; draft a set of in-service training and examination questions to test a broad range of relevant interpretation skills. Thomas Chong: Large language generative models can be helpful in situations where text follows a predictable pattern. Currently, these tools could be used in low-risk areas such as formatting and grammar in reports, policies, and procedures. They can be used for operational and administrative purposes, such as summarization of email threads and workflows, improving the lab help call center, guiding users through procedures, and simplifying medical notes and comments for the layperson. In anatomic pathology, ChatGPT can help rewrite a complex autopsy clinical-pathological correlation summary so that it is more understandable to the next-of-kin. Language models could be combined with image generative models to help visualize the morphological progression of disease over time (e.g., cervical dysplasia) or of physiologic processes (e.g., hematopoiesis). Tissue features on a slide only provide a snapshot in time of one patient’s pathologic progression that has been inferred from many patients. Generative models could help visualize the progression through the continuum between states, in a manner beyond mere interpolation of static images. This perspective could be a boon for quickly understanding what otherwise might only have been gained through hundreds of hours of slide review. It could also lead to new insights that may not be readily observable in a snapshot. What is driving the rapid improvement of these models? If this improvement continues, what new opportunities for laboratory application might arise? Brian Jackson: These very large-scale models require extraordinary levels of computing power, which has only recently become feasible (and only feasible for certain well-funded and technologically capable organizations). Developers happen to be on a steep part of the S-curve where they can show rapid improvement in generating human-like language responses. There’s no guarantee that the models will continue to improve rapidly in other areas that are important to us as humans, particularly trustworthiness, accuracy, and reliability. Also, we should keep in mind that there are historic examples of mind-blowing technologies that remained niche applications, not transformative, such as Segway, Siri, and personal jet packs. Jonathan H. Chen: Many of the advances have been based on the sheer scale of the systems being produced in terms of the number of parameters the underlying models learn and the internet scale datasets they are trained on. There will eventually be practical and technical limits to how far pure scale can reach. Much of the demonstrated capability of emerging chatbot systems is based not just on the “autocomplete on steroids” underlying model but additional layers of supervised learning and reinforcement learning with human feedback. In these latter cases, humans provide the language models examples of what a good answer to an example question should look like, as well as a relative rating of how much a human likes the answers these systems give to help them better address prompts, align with human interest and intent, and avoid toxic or otherwise adverse responses. It's likely that we cannot accurately predict, and can only speculate, what the future potential of such systems might be. The current pace of change and new applications being discovered is moving faster than can be easily tracked. Thomas Chong: Arguably, the relatively rapid improvement in the performance of large language models (LLMs) can be attributed to the industry's efforts to increase their scale. However, such efforts may not address their inherent weaknesses. Immediate improvements made to existing LLM systems may be more evolutionary than revolutionary. Generative models could be utilized to automate safe actions, such as sending an email or text message alert and scheduling meetings. Also, integration with voice-to-text and text-to-voice technology appears inevitable. Opportunities exist in application-specific training of these tools, allowing for local execution and integration with local medical record databases. This would be necessary to protect personal health information. Custom data report generation and deployment could be expedited by LLM-assist in the back-end development for SQL query generation, in the front-end development of custom code-based data visualizations, and creating/following workflows for data validation and quality control. Also, models trained on specialist domain-specific knowledge might prove to be useful, although validation of such a resource would be challenging. Jason Baron: Taking the second question, we might imagine shorter term applications such as clinician facing chatbots to help with logistical questions around laboratory test ordering and result reporting, replacing some, but not all, the work of laboratory call centers. We might have algorithms supporting quality control/quality assurance review, monitoring budgets, automatically placing service calls, drafting standard operating procedures (for human review), and organizing documents for CLIA inspections. Longer term, I would imagine algorithms truly supporting more clinical functions such as helping clinicians select optimal laboratory tests and interpret their results considering the patient-specific medical record. There are certainly knowledgeable people who are predicting this technology will achieve human-like intelligence within the coming decades. Neither I nor anyone knows with certainty if or when this will happen; if it does, it would of course be a game changer not only for the lab but for any type of knowledge work and likely life in general. Regardless, it is hard for me to imagine a world in my lifetime where an AI is legally allowed to be the CLIA director or technical supervisor. Acknowledging that most laboratorians will not possess a deep understanding of how generative AI models produce outputs and that these models can be opaque, would it be irresponsible to use these models within laboratory medicine? But, in most of those cases, the technology is trustworthy and reliable, with performance that is highly predictable to experts in that field. titulo: A Systematic Review of AI-Assisted Code Generation in Regulated Software Environments: Reliability, Governance, and Compliance Implications
resumo: Large language models now write a material and growing share of production software, including software that executes regulated financial functions.The empirical literature on their reliability has grown rapidly and is, on its own terms, sophisticated.The governance frameworks that regulated institutions must satisfy were, without exception, written for a different kind of artefact, and in the most consequential recent case, were revised in full knowledge of generative AI and deliberately declined to cover it.Objective.This review synthesises the evidence on the reliability of AI-assisted code generation, on the human factors governing its use, and on the intellectual-property and supply-chain exposures it creates; and determines how that evidence maps onto the model-risk, AI-specific and operational-resilience regimes applicable to regulated software environments.Method.We conducted a systematic literature review following Kitchenham et al. and reported against PRISMA 2020, with a restricted multivocal stratum after Garousi et al. admitting regulatory instruments and supervisory guidance.Studies were appraised on an adapted Dybå-Dingsøyr instrument extended with an item recording whether deployment context or regulatory constraint is characterised.Results.Five findings.First, benchmark performance and field reliability have decoupled: correctness benchmarks are saturated and contamination-prone while defect rates measured in real repositories remain substantial, so the headline capability numbers do not license deployment inferences.Second, security evidence is mixed, controlled model evaluations report high vulnerability rates while several developer studies find little or no security penalty, and the disagreement is explained by unit of analysis rather than by any study being wrong.Third, the most robust human-factors finding is not that assisted code is worse but that developers believe it is better than it is, which relocates the risk from the artefact to the review process.Fourth, package hallucination converts a model reliability property into an attacker-controllable supply-chain channel, and is the one exposure with no human-review mitigation.Fifth, and most consequentially, the April 2026 revision of US interagency model-risk guidance explicitly excludes generative and agentic AI from scope, leaving the primary supervisory framework silent on precisely this class of system. A Systematic Review of AI-Assisted Code Generation in Regulated Software Environments: Reliability, Governance, and ComplianceImplications; David Excel Ozowara Conclusion.We argue that AI-assisted code generation is misclassified when treated as a model-risk problem, because the model produces no decision and enters no inventory; it is better understood as a change to the software development lifecycle's assurance basis.We present the Generated Code Assurance Frame, a five-layer mapping from generation practice to the assurance claim it disturbs, and a research agenda centred on measuring review efficacy rather than generation quality.Citation

titulo: Class‐Rheum for AI : Reflections from a Filipino Rheumatologist and Health Informatics graduate student
resumo: In 2019, when I returned to the university for my master's studies in Health Informatics, we had no subject particular to artificial intelligence (AI). A pandemic and a few theses proposal delays later, we're learning about AI more voraciously than ever: studying the literature, listening to online podcasts, organizing lectures, and coffee meeting groups with the Department of Computer Science. I am grateful to receive knowledge from my more experienced international colleagues, in the meantime1, 2 but as a graduate student, I am still an explorer. An explorer, since I am only the third Filipino Rheumatologist in Health Informatics, caught amid a country undergoing a socio-technical transition.3 Despite the challenges of this transition such as partial implementation and selective participation of stakeholders, many of my colleagues in Health Informatics are frontline, leaders, and drivers of this change. But before AI can even take place, the Philippines must digitize its healthcare services as part of the plan to provide universal healthcare.4 My institution began plans for digitization only in 2019 and became hospital-wide for one of its branches only in 2021.5 As an aspiring informatician, I was able to participate in this milestone—continuously addressing resistance, determining better workflows, and identifying clinical implications. By 2024, it is hoped that the same electronic records will be available in its other branches in the north part of the capital. It seems, therefore, that being an informatics student, and a rheumatologist, I am running on two treadmills at once. However, even if many of our local hospitals have not yet fully digitized, AI will not be waiting for us to catch up, as it is already permeating through everything as we speak. We continue to use our smartphone (or two), without realizing AI is already inside. The recently concluded Asia Pacific League for Rheumatology in Thailand was already using an AI in the congress app, and some did not even notice.6 It identifies the delegate's preferred topic of interest and recommends other sessions they may like or recommend colleagues with similar interests they may want to connect with. Facebook chat stickers can now be customized by AI, if the stock stickers and gifs just aren't sending the message you want.7 Perhaps the travel app is already suggesting your next itinerary based on your interests and past travels. Who knows, our shopping app will soon add-to-cart certain products for you since we always shop during this week of the month. It's here, it's happening, but where do I, an early career rheumatologist, graduate student and aspiring researcher-informatician, stand under all of this? Allow me to gather my thoughts on my current three rheumatologist roles: as a clinician, as a student (or early researcher), and as a teacher. As a clinical rheumatologist, I welcome the opportunity for assistance in clinic or hospital tasks. However, we are also decreasing in terms of workforce number as a specialty and because of the Pandemic, as doctors in general.8-10 We need rapid identification or assessment of conditions in order not to delay treatment. Much rheumatologic research has been shown to be promising in radiographs,11 magnetic resonance imaging,12 and even musculoskeletal ultrasound.13, 14 All the above may be useful for countries that don't have enough imaging subspecialists. Phenotyping conditions like mixed connective tissue disease because of their diverse presentations can also help determine the best course treatment.15 Digitizing our medical records may help us in predicting disease activity flares before they even manifest16-18 preventing high costs of admissions or needing an intensive care unit. Identifying social media perceptions of patients19 may also help improve communication during outpatient consults. Due to the growing numbers of articles published daily, it is becoming progressively more challenging to keep up with the output. Almost every assignment during my classes needed an extensive literature review, while navigating the infodemic. Search engines have been evolving in this aspect: Research papers can be compared and arranged in a visual network, organize citation, and compare contradicting and supporting concepts.20 My personal favorites have been researchrabbit.org and connectedpapers.com. However, in the year since I did a talk about these at our local annual conference; many others have been released in various development stages, such as chatpdf, scite.ai, and elicit.org. Likewise, when you do research, you also produce output. Clinical Abstracts have now evolved from text predominant busy slides, to more visually appealing, but static infographics and now to abstracts with audio.20 This will increase the content available not only for AI search engines but also for the random internet citizen looking for the right information. As the pandemic restrictions ease, we also see the return of in-person participation in conferences. During the Lupus – Korean College of Rheumatology Conference in May 2023, simultaneous translations by live interpreters were available. As an amateur student of Korean (and other languages) myself, I found this amazing. In a multicultural, multi-island region with diverse languages that predominantly don't use Roman letters, I envision a future APLAR conference where AI can destroy the language barrier in science. We won't have to miss out on talented researchers who may be uncomfortable with conventional English. We may also feel less awkward in initiating and accepting international collaborations.21 The loss of the hybrid versions warrants another long discussion for another day. Medical education is also currently being challenged by AI.22 AIs connected to image-generating programs such as DALL-E have been shown to have some use in our related specialties: radiology and dermatology medical education.23, 24 It would be interesting to explore these interactions in a patient perspective type of study. We also need to examine our current pedagogy—MCQs alone may no longer be enough to evaluate student or trainee understanding.25-27 As an introduction to AI in Medicine, I also agree that we should include these LLMs during clinicopathological conferences. These may give med students and trainees an opportunity to develop critical thinking by identifying its weaknesses and strengths—and propose solutions with or without the collaboration of Computer Science colleagues. Some examples of the proper way to conduct these conferences can be seen in the work of Rodman et al.28, 29 I often get asked whether I am not concerned about being replaced or about AI “over-dependence”—and of humanity losing certain skills. Arthur C Clarke, science-fiction writer and futurist, said in an old documentary that he does not find the idea upsetting and that we (whomever the present humanity is) should regard it a privilege to be a “steppingstone”—as we have done so for the Cro-Magnon.30 I agree—we shouldn't consider it as losing. I could “lose” the skill to memorize certain phone numbers, records of patients, laboratory results, etc. But it may give me the opportunity to learn something new, like a new language perhaps or a new skill—like learning Python programming maybe? There's always something rejuvenating about returning to the university. But wherever this is going, I hope we'll always make rheum for new knowledge. Lisa S. titulo: Opinion: Mental health research: to augment or not to augment
resumo: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) into healthcare is growing, with tools often limited by data scarcity and biases; issues particularly pronounced in mental health research. Data augmentation, a method of artificially expanding datasets, holds promise for addressing these challenges by creating synthetic data, improving diversity, and reducing costs. This has shown success in medical imaging, yet mental health datasets face unique barriers, including subjective measurements, privacy concerns, and underrepresentation of marginalized groups. Augmented data can help balance these datasets, enhance diagnostic accuracy, and improve generalizability, enabling more equitable AI models. However, risks such as replicating existing biases, losing cultural context, and producing clinically unreliable augmented data require careful consideration. In mental health, small variations in data can influence outcomes significantly, and poorly designed augmentation could oversimplify complex experiences. To harmonize potential with caution, augmented data should complement real-world data and be rigorously evaluated by clinicians for alignment with expertise. Ethical implications, including consent and privacy, demand careful frameworks to ensure augmented datasets are responsibly used. While data augmentation offers exciting opportunities to advance mental health research, its implementation must prioritize transparency, clinical fidelity, and equity.In recent years, there has been significant growth in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in healthcare. AI-based tools are increasingly used to predict diagnoses, personalize treatment plans, and assess risk factors, aiming to enable more scalable mental health care solutions. However, mental health research is often limited by the availability of highquality and large sample datasets and confounded by the multifaceted complexities of human behaviors and emotions. 1 To address this gap, researchers have begun to utilize data augmentation techniques to expand available datasets. Generating new data artificially enables models to use larger and more complete training datasets. Consider the medical imaging field, where AI has become a prominent fixture in practice. Data augmentation has demonstrated benefits across all organs and modalities to help promote medical imaging training without investing time and resources into collecting new samples. 2 However, mental health research presents many unique barriers to integrating data augmentation. Biases inherent in the original set of mental health data remain and can result in overfitting where a model is unable to make accurate predictions from any other data other than the training data. This article explores the unique challenges researchers must overcome due to the lack of representative mental health data and how these challenges interact with AI and ML advancements. We explore data augmentation as a tool to bridge this gap, offering an integrative perspective on the ethical and practical challenges. As researchers consider data augmentation in mental health research, it is critical to evaluate the promise through rigorous methodologies and research and decide whether 'to augment or not to augment'.As AI and ML algorithms have advanced exponentially in recent years, one of the most prominent limiting factors remains the availability of representative training data that determines model performance. 3 In contrast to synthetic data that creates data from scratch, data augmentation is an ML technique used to create new data based on existing data points, thereby artificially expanding a dataset. There are several data augmentation methods, with some incorporating simple transformations to text data (rotating images by random degrees, flipping images horizontally, and back-translation of data to a new language). Expanding on this, generative adversarial network (GAN) based augmentation is a more sophisticated strategy that uses neural networks to create novel samples from a pre-existing dataset. For example, GANs can augment data for chest X-rays that not only improve classification accuracy but perform better than other simple transformation methods. 4 Large language models (LLMs), such as GPT-4o, have also been used for clinical transcript data augmentation. 5 With various strategies available, data augmentation can be a potential tool for all fields of medical research moving forward. Augmentation can address class imbalance while preserving anonymity, facilitating cross-lingual and robust mental health research with available data. While data augmentation may enhance model generalizability and facilitate new research, mental health research introduces concerns about augmentation because of unique challenges in balancing realism and mitigating biases.To Augment: Overcoming Data Scarceness Data scarcity remains a significant challenge in mental health research. Unlike other areas of medicine that can evaluate objective data from available biomarkers and imaging, mental health research relies on qualitative interviews, self-reported surveys, questionnaires, and clinical notes. The subjective nature of mental health concepts, such as emotional well-being, 6 also makes developing universally accepted definitions challenging. Despite self-reported measurements being cost-efficient, flexible, and valuable for uncovering personal perceptions, 7 many datasets do not provide the comprehensive, diverse, and sufficient data necessary for generalizable and reliable research. Furthermore, data collection is hindered by high costs, privacy concerns, stigma, and recruitment difficulties. Augmented data presents a promising opportunity to address these issues. By artificially generating new data, such as augmented text or audio, researchers can increase usable data, mitigate the concerns of dependency on subjective reports of experiences, and enhance the scalability of mental health studies. 8 Data augmentation is a cost-effective alternative to collecting new clinical data, reducing the reliance on expensive longitudinal studies. By using augmented data, researchers may limit the reliance on personally identifiable information, enhancing privacy protection. As well, researchers can instead focus efforts on generating new insights and testing hypotheses using readily available datasets. Mental health datasets are often highly imbalanced, with certain conditions underrepresented (e.g., borderline personality disorder) compared to others (e.g., depression), and gender disparities in diagnosis, treatment, and research. Rare mental health disorders can present with uncommon symptoms, which can complicate diagnoses. 9 Moreover, certain populations-such as children, seniors, racial minorities, LGBTQ2+, and marginalized groups-are also underrepresented in datasets. This imbalance can lead to biased conclusions and unreliable predictive models, which can perpetuate disparities and further marginalize underserved populations. Addressing these issues, data augmentation can create more balanced datasets by artificially increasing the representation of minority classes, allowing ML models to better detect and treat underrepresented conditions and populations. AI-generated data can impute missing information and ensure datasets are more diverse, leading to more inclusive and equitable models. For instance, psychiatric symptoms often manifest differently across age groups and genders, with adolescents and adults experiencing distinct presentations of similar conditions. 10 Augmented data allows for a better representation of subgroups, which can enhance diagnostic accuracy and treatment outcomes. Augmentation is also crucial in scaling AI models. Introducing synthetic variations, such as noise injection, makes models more robust and less prone to overfitting. This increased variability enables models to learn general patterns rather than memorizing specific instances, thus improving their generalizability across different patient groups. This is particularly beneficial in mental health research, where there is significant variability in behavior and emotions. For example, consider a research team studying depressive disorders in a population skewed towards high symptom severity levels. An ML model trained on this real-world data may not predict accurate outcomes when applied to patient groups with lower symptom severity levels. 11 However, researchers can achieve more accurate and generalizable predictions by generating augmented data that mimics these underrepresented cases. 12 Incorporating data augmentation could improve research and clinical practice outcomes, allowing decision-support tools to be developed, and offering more equitable recommendations. Not To Augment: Bias and Clinician Fidelity Mental health data is nuanced and profoundly contextual, with small variations in symptoms or patient perceptions potentially leading to different clinical outcomes. This type of data has multifactorial and complicated biological, psychological, and social components. One of the most significant risks of data augmentation is replicating and potentially amplifying biases present in the original datasets. If the original dataset underrepresents certain cultural, gender, or ethnic groups, these biases may be further embedded into the model. Poorly designed augmented data, if not inspected by mental health professionals, may fail to respect the nuanced interplay of different symptomatology and can mistakenly intensify biases present in the original dataset, which may also introduce new biases. 13,14 In mental health research, historical biases regarding race, gender, and socioeconomic status are well-documented and must be mitigated. 15 Creating augmented data may risk the loss of meaning, especially when nuanced cultural and individual differences are simplified. This could lead to generalized stereotypes or poor representation of complex mental health experiences. 16 Augmented data may fail to consider the complexity of identities intersecting such factors, which may result in inaccurate predictions, leading to inconsistencies in treatment recommendations. This is especially problematic in mental health, where symptoms and coping mechanisms can vary greatly across cultures due to differences in language, values, and stigma around mental illness. Augmented data generated without consideration of cultural contexts might promote the development of AI models that misinterpret the mental health challenges of underrepresented populations. Traditional augmentation techniques may treat diverse groups as homogeneous, reducing cultural and ethnic variability to a few representative data points, thus risking generalization and misrepresentation. Moreover, augmented data may lack clinical expertise and the ability to reproduce real-world patient behavior and presentation. 17 Augmented data may oversimplify the variability that clinicians rely on for diagnosis and treatment. Adding synthetic noise or random data augmentation may alter key data features, causing a loss of context crucial to understanding mental health conditions. For example, AI-generated text transcripts of patient interviews might lack the subtle linguistic cues and emotional context necessary for a clinician's judgment. 18 This disconnect could result in models that appear highly accurate in theory but fail to translate into reliable real-world clinical support. Evaluating the quality of augmented data is particularly challenging in mental health due to the subjective nature of psychological assessments and a lack of consistent validation benchmarks.Given the different perspectives in this argument, how should mental health research proceed with augmented data? The key is cautious optimism. While augmented data should not be dismissed outright, it must be integrated with real-world data in a way that preserves transparency and mitigates bias. One approach is to utilize augmented data to supplement rather than replace real-world data. Combining both traditional and augmented datasets can enhance the dataset diversity without over-relying on synthetic information. Models trained on augmented data should also be evaluated by mental health professionals with standard accuracy metrics and qualitative appraisals. This will help ensure that augmented data-driven predictions align with clinical expertise and judgment. To integrate augmented data into mental health research effectively, researchers should prioritize pilot and feasibility studies to assess its practicality and ensure alignment with clinical expertise. Collaborative efforts based on these findings can also address challenges related to bias, equity, and implementation. Societal and cultural norms heavily influence how mental health symptoms are expressed, understood, and treated. For example, some cultures may emphasize physical symptoms like headaches, while others focus on emotional or behavioural aspects. 19 Data augmentation preserves the distributional properties of the original dataset, including those with small sample sizes, imbalances, or underrepresented features. By enhancing the diversity and representation within the dataset, models trained on well-augmented data are more likely to generalize effectively and exhibit reduced bias. Importantly, if cultural nuances are present in the original data but captured unevenly, data augmentation can help balance representation. This allows the model to better generalize across cultural subtleties, improving its fairness and applicability. Incorporating ethnographic insights or consulting cultural experts during data creation can further improve augmented data's realism and applicability. 20 The financial implications of data augmentation are an important consideration in promoting global health equity. Researchers in wealthier regions often have greater access to the tools and funding, potentially exacerbating inequalities. 21 In contrast, researchers in underserved areas may face significant barriers to adopting these technologies. Open Science initiatives could help promote the sharing of augmented datasets and tools, enabling broader access. 21,22 Publicly available platforms can democratize research opportunities, while transparency protocols requiring researchers to disclose their augmentation methods could foster collaboration and reduce disparities. By addressing these financial and equity concerns, the benefits of augmented data can be distributed more equitably across research communities. 22 Finally, the ethical implications of using augmented data in mental health research must not be overlooked. Augmented data can mitigate privacy concerns however, generating realistic patient data raises questions about consent and transparency. In addition, ethicists will need to develop clear guidelines for using augmented data in healthcare AI models that align with clinicians' preferred practices and optimize patient confidentiality. Frameworks that promote positive clinician-AI interactions can ensure that AI data-driven models undertake the same rigorous inspection as models based on real-world data and be successfully implemented in clinical settings. 23,24 The use of augmented data in mental health research is an exciting frontier, contributing to the potential to overcome long-standing challenges of data scarcity and imbalance. Data augmentation has been demonstrated to be a useful tool in other medical fields, such as medical imaging. However, introducing augmented data into the mental health field must be handled with caution. While the promise of enhanced model performance and data diversity is desirable, the risks of bias, unreliability, and ethical concerns may limit feasibility.We extend our gratitude to the researchers and clinicians whose foundational work on data augmentation and mental health inspired this commentary. Special thanks to the Interventional Psychiatry Program lab members at St. Michael's Hospital for their valuable insights and feedback.

titulo: 光计算技术在智能时代的现状、挑战与未来（特邀）
resumo: In the era of rapid development of artificial intelligence and deep learning technologies, complex algorithms represented by large language models have led to an exponential growth in computing power demand. However, traditional electronic computing architectures are facing a dual dilemma: on one hand, semiconductor process nodes are approaching the physical limit, resulting in diminishing performance gains from transistor size reduction, while the cost and difficulty of each process upgrade continue to rise; on the other hand, the energy consumption problem of data centers has become increasingly acute, and the energy efficiency wall has emerged as a core obstacle hindering the continuous improvement of computing power. Against this backdrop, the paradigm of photonic computing, which uses light as the information carrier, has emerged. With its inherent capabilities of high-speed parallel processing, ultra-low energy consumption, and multi-dimensional information encoding, it offers a revolutionary solution to break through the computing power bottleneck.There exists an innate compatibility between optical computing and AI algorithms, rooted in the deep congruence of their computational paradigms. Core operations in neural networks, such as matrix multiplication and vector convolution, are essentially large-scale parallel processing tasks. The wave nature and spatial parallel propagation characteristics of photons provide an ideal physical implementation platform for these operations. Compared with the switching speed of electrons in semiconductor devices, optical signals can complete cross-dimensional information interaction within an extremely short time scale, and the energy consumption per bit of information processing is far lower than that of electronic devices. This technological advantage has reshaped the computing ecosystem in three key dimensions: in terms of computational efficiency, traditional computing processors based on the von Neumann architecture suffer from the inherent flaw of separating storage from computation, leading to a disproportionately high energy consumption for data transfer. In contrast, optical computing, through integrated photonic neural networks, can perform real-time matrix operations on optical signals on silicon photonics chips, effectively eliminating the data transfer bottleneck. Regarding energy efficiency ratio, photonic devices can process multiple optical signals in parallel on a single chip, achieving a significant improvement in energy efficiency ratio compared to GPUs in typical tasks like image recognition. This characteristic is of vital importance for energy-constrained scenarios such as edge computing and the Internet of Things. In terms of environmental adaptability, optical signal transmission is immune to electromagnetic interference, and its stability far exceeds that of electronic devices in extreme environments such as high temperatures and strong radiation, endowing it with irreplaceable advantages in demanding fields like aerospace and military communications.Currently, although traditional electronic computing still dominates the field of general-purpose computing power, optical computing, with its unique advantages, has become an indispensable part of heterogeneous computing architectures. The academic and industrial sectors are vigorously promoting the engineering implementation of photonic computing technology. From the continuous maturation of silicon photonics integration processes to the ongoing innovation of hybrid optoelectronic architectures, from the breakthroughs in the development of dedicated AI chips to the active exploration of photonic neuromorphic computing, photonic computing is gradually transitioning from the theoretical verification stage to the critical period of commercial application.This comprehensive review traces the technological evolution of optical computing for neural network acceleration, systematically covering both linear and nonlinear computational frameworks. Within linear optical computing architectures, three core devices stand out with distinct advantages: Programmable Mach-Zehnder Interferometers enable large-scale reconfigurable matrix operations through precise phase modulation of optical signals, leveraging their inherent parallelism to adapt dynamically to varying neural network layer requirements. Micro-ring resonators, excel in multi-wavelength high-integration scenarios—their wavelength-division multiplexing capability allows simultaneous processing of multiple data streams on a single chip, achieving high-density parallelism with minimal crosstalk, a critical feature for compact photonic computing systems. Spatial diffractive optical elements harness wavefront manipulation to realize high spatial parallelism, executing ultra-large-scale vector convolutions essential for visual computing tasks without the constraints of waveguide losses, thus maximizing throughput in spatial information processing. In the realm of nonlinear optical computing, optical nonlinear activation functions emerge as the pivotal breakthrough for unlocking photonic neural network performance. Evolving from early hybrid optoelectronic implementations to cutting-edge all-optical solutions integrated on silicon photonics platforms, these functions now exhibit dynamic reconfigurability and ultra-low power consumption. This progression has overcome the fundamental limitation of linear optical systems in replicating the complex nonlinear behaviors of biological neural networks, significantly enhancing network expressivity and enabling more accurate emulation of brain-like computational paradigms.Nevertheless, the large-scale application of optical computing technology still faces numerous formidable challenges. At the level of optical devices, the current integration density and stability fail to meet the requirements of large-scale commercial applications, and issues such as coupling losses between devices, thermal stability, and long-term reliability urgently need to be addressed. During all-optical signal processing, noise control and precision optimization remain key technical difficulties restricting the performance improvement of optical computing. Additionally, the compatibility between optical computing systems and the existing electronic ecosystem cannot be overlooked. Achieving efficient data interaction and collaborative operation between optical and electronic computing is a crucial step in promoting the widespread application of optical computing technology. Looking ahead, with the continuous refinement of silicon photonics integration processes, the continuous innovation of hybrid optoelectronic architectures, and the in-depth advancement of interdisciplinary research, the deep integration and collaborative innovation of optical and electronic computing will surely become the key path to breaking through the computing power bottleneck and building green and efficient computing power infrastructure. Optical computing technology will comprehensively reshape the intelligent computing ecosystem, providing powerful computing support for the development of AI, playing a significant role in numerous fields such as autonomous driving, financial technology, and weather forecasting, and propelling human intelligent computing technology to a new stage of development.

resumo: The climate crisis poses a critical threat to health systems and populations globally, with projections of 14.5 million preventable deaths and $1.1 trillion in healthcare costs by 2050.1 The pace at which the climate is destabilizing is accelerating.2 Global temperatures could rise more than 2°C above preindustrial levels by mid-century, a tipping point beyond which climate impacts may outpace capacity for adaptation.3 The relationship between climate change and health is well established. Further, climate-driven catastrophes threaten continuous care delivery by disrupting supply chains, straining or destroying critical healthcare physical and social infrastructure, increasing costs and care demand by adding and exacerbating disease burden, and negatively impacting overall quality and access to care. At the same time, the healthcare sector itself is a major emitter of environmental pollutants, contributing nearly 5% to total global greenhouse gas emissions and inflicting 4.5 million disability adjusted life-years in health harms each year from its air pollution alone.4 The healthcare sector must mitigate its own environmental impact while simultaneously strengthening its ability to meet escalating threats to health and care delivery posed by the climate crisis.5 To help address this crucial challenge, the Yale Center on Climate Change and Health and The New York Academy of Medicine instituted an annual conference focusing on sustainable healthcare system transformation. The inaugural event, “Health Systems Implementing Climate Action,” took place on September 27, 2024, during Climate Week NYC, in tandem with the United Nations General Assembly. The conference brought together leaders from the health and business sectors to discuss the latest experiences and research findings on several themes: low-carbon, resilient healthcare delivery; ensuring healthcare infrastructure resilience to climate impacts; preparing the healthcare workforce for climate impacts; the role of health insurers in meeting climate risks; engaging government and philanthropic funders to support healthcare resilience and pollution mitigation; and addressing the rise of greenwashing in the healthcare sector. See Table 1 for a complete list of topics and speakers. The insights and strategies presented during the panel discussions and keynote presentations, summarized below, provide guidance for implementing climate action in healthcare to build and scale up sustainable health systems. Githinji Gitahi, MBBS, Global CEO of Amref Health Africa Closing Remarks SETTING THE STAGE: FINDINGS FROM THE 2024 LANCET COUNTDOWN Key findings from the Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change underscore the pace and severity of climate-related health threats and healthcare’s contribution.6 Heat-related mortality among adults older than 65 years has increased 167% since the 1990s. Drought and heatwaves are driving food insecurity, with 127 million more people experiencing moderate to severe impacts in recent years. Climate-sensitive infectious diseases such as malaria and dengue are spreading into new geographic areas, including highland regions and parts of Europe and North America. These risks are converging, intensifying existing pressures on overstretched health systems and compounding vulnerabilities in settings with limited adaptive capacity. Healthcare systems are also major contributors to the crisis. Global healthcare emissions have risen 36% since 2016 and now account for nearly 5% of total greenhouse gas emissions. In many high-income countries, healthcare system emissions now greatly exceed the point at which additional spending generates any further health gains, revealing systemic overconsumption and missed opportunities for sustainable care. Healthcare systems must be reimagined to reduce emissions while improving care access and high-quality outcomes. These findings make clear that healthcare must play a central role in both responding to and helping to stabilize the climate crisis. Cities, Facilities, and Utilities: Healthcare Infrastructure Mitigation, Adaptation, and Resilience More than half the global population currently resides in cities, a figure projected to reach 70% by 2050.7 Developing sustainable, climate-ready cities therefore is key to supporting healthier populations and ecosystems. Ensuring healthcare and public health systems are integrated into adaptation planning is vital, yet cities have been slow to incorporate health into their climate strategies. A report by the Yale School of Public Health, Resilient Cities Network, and The Rockefeller Foundation found that, although 44% of cities have resilience plans, only 27% address health comprehensively.8 Through strategic partnerships, city administrators and public health and healthcare leaders will be better positioned to implement and fund data-driven solutions to strengthen infrastructure, protect vulnerable populations, increase health system resilience, and reduce its contribution to an unstable climate. Urban centers are responsible for 75% of global emissions, driving significant climate-related health and care risks.7–9 These risks include physical trauma, heat- and smoke-related illnesses, vector-borne and waterborne diseases, and mental health challenges.10–18 Extreme weather events such as floods, hurricanes, wildfires, and heatwaves can disrupt infrastructure and supply chains that healthcare systems depend on, jeopardizing ongoing patient care and emergency response capabilities.19 Poorly designed or outdated facilities are vulnerable to power outages, water contamination, and structural damage, resulting in service interruptions. Collaboration between city, public health, and healthcare system administrators is essential to plan for and develop resilient infrastructure capable of withstanding these climate-related challenges, to ensure continuous care delivery.20–22 The healthcare sector must take responsibility for reducing its carbon footprint.23–26 Healthcare systems can significantly reduce emissions by transitioning to renewable energy, optimizing energy and resource use, and environmentally preferable purchasing. titulo: Abstracts from the 2025 ADLM Preanalytical Phase Conference—Advancing Preanalytics: From Innovative Breakthroughs to Practical Applications
resumo: The preanalytical phase of laboratory testing remains a critical and persistently complex component of the total testing process. Unlike the analytical phase, which benefits from robust quality control systems, the preanalytical phase is inherently less amenable to traditional quality assurance strategies due to the multitude of variables that can affect specimen integrity. Factors include patient preparation, specimen collection, handling, transport, and processing. This phase is further complicated by the involvement of a diverse array of practitioners, including phlebotomists, nursing staff, clinicians, and couriers. Adding further complexity is the desire to increase access to laboratory testing by placing specimen collection into homes and other unconventional, non-healthcare settings, performed by the patient themselves. The distributed responsibility introduces additional complexity and variability, underscoring the need for ongoing education, collaboration, and process improvement (1). Challenges maintaining a competent and robust workforce contribute to vacancies for laboratory professionals ranging up to 25%, with some specialties and regions experiencing even higher shortages (2). These staffing shortages have direct implications for laboratory quality and patient care, including increased turnaround times, risk of errors, and reduced access to timely diagnostics. Many institutions faced with staffing shortages and budget constraints are having to do more with less, which has ushered in an era of desire to increase automation and use digital tools to help alleviate the clerical burden with the hope of improving staff satisfaction and retention as well as the quality of the testing process. The integration of informatics, automation, and artificial intelligence offers promising avenues for error reduction, yet also introduces new challenges that require vigilant oversight and continuous innovation (3). The 2025 Association for Diagnostics & Laboratory Medicine (ADLM) Preanalytical Phase Conference, held in Providence, RI, continued a tradition of addressing the ever-present and evolving challenges in the preanalytical phase of laboratory medicine. Building on previous conferences in Alexandria and Philadelphia (Table 1), ADLM welcomed about 130 attendees from 11 countries and 30 US states. This year’s program brought together leading experts to explore practical solutions and future innovations to improve and expand specimen collection opportunities as well as technological advancements. Title, venue and dates of the four Association for Diagnostics & Laboratory Medicine (ADLM) preanalytical conferences. 2019 AACC Preanalytical Phase Conference “Optimizing Quality in the Clinical Laboratory: Focus on the Preanalytical Phase.” Alexandria, VA. November 11–12, 2019 2022 AACC Preanalytical Phase Conference “Reducing Errors and Improving Quality in the Preanalytical Phase: The Role of the Laboratory.” Alexandria, VA. June 3–4, 2022 2023 AACC Preanalytical Phase Conference “Implementing Preanalytical Tools That Improve Patient Care.” Philadelphia, PA. October 21, 2023 2025 ADLM Preanalytical Phase Conference “Advancing Preanalytics: From Innovative Breakthroughs to Practical Applications.” Providence, RI. October 23–24, 2025 The conference opened with a keynote presented by Mark A. Zaydman, MD, PhD from Washington University in St. Louis, MO, focusing on the transformative potential of artificial intelligence in preanalytical processes. Session 1 continued the innovation theme with presentations focused on new and novel ways and places to collect clinical specimens (Table 2), with an emphasis on expanding patient access to laboratory testing. Session 2 addressed preanalytical issues with specimens collected for hematology, coagulation, molecular, and urinalysis testing (Table 2). Session 3 transitioned to the very practical, dealing with essentials in preanalytics aimed at addressing errors which most laboratories struggle with, including minimizing draw volumes, optimizing hemolysis, and designing dashboards to monitor preanalytical quality metrics (Table 2). The closing keynote presented by Frederick Strathmann, PhD, MBA, DABCC (MOBILion Systems) taught the audience about different personality styles and how this knowledge of ourselves and others can be used for effective communication to build successful multidisciplinary teams. Program and faculty for the 2025 ADLM Preanalytical Conference. Breakout sessions provided interactive opportunities for participants to engage with conference faculty, which included a rousing game of “Phlebotomy Jeopardy” and even a “Serum vs Plasma Showdown” in addition to effective communication strategies, work flow analysis and sample routing, assessing fairness in preanalytics, and handling of remotely collected samples (Table 2). The conference also featured 28 peer-reviewed posters submitted by conference participants, which we are pleased to share in this edition of JALM (see Supplemental Material). These posters addressed improvements in specimen collection practices, reduction of hemolysis and contamination, detection, evaluation and mitigation of preanalytical interferences, optimization of transport and processing work flows, and the use of informatics and automation to support quality improvement. Collectively, the poster presentations illustrated the robust and ongoing efforts across institutions to strengthen preanalytical reliability, expand innovative collection models, and enhance the overall quality of diagnostic testing. The 2025 ADLM Preanalytical Phase Conference exemplifies the field’s commitment to advancing laboratory medicine through collaboration, innovation, and education. By convening experts to address persistent and emerging challenges—from hemolysis and interferences to the integration of artificial intelligence and remote collection models—the conference fostered a desire to learn from colleagues and take away practical solutions to common problems, as well as providing a venue to explore the future of preanalytics. Its established position within ADLM underscores the importance of the preanalytical phase in ensuring the high quality which diagnostic laboratory medicine provides. As laboratory medicine continues to adapt to new technologies and care models, the insights and strategies shared at this conference will be instrumental in shaping the future of preanalytics and enhancing patient outcomes. The success of the 2025 ADLM Preanalytical Phase Conference reflects the dedication and expertise of its faculty, the thoughtful leadership of the organizing committee and ADLM staff, the generous support of our industry sponsor, and the active engagement of each attendee and poster presenter.
